description:
超微今年不一樣了: four students from NCUE, Taiwan (Dun Jie Yang, Chang Sheng-Lin, Tseng Yun-Chen, Cheng-Hsun Liu).

Why "Keeling"? Charles David Keeling's CO2 record shows a seasonal cycle on top of a slow trend. Our tool looks past the season to find the trend. A tribute; his data is not used.

What it does: a web globe that asks four questions of NASA records: what is changing, where, how much, and is it significant? Every trend comes with its uncertainty.
summary: Keeling is a web globe that turns NASA Earth-observation time series into something a student or a curious reader can question. It shows twelve variables of water, heat, air and plants (from GPM IMERG, GLDAS, AIRS, MERRA-2, OMI and MODIS) at five places in Taiwan, twelve world cities and as a global mean, plus global trend maps for seven variables. For every series it answers the four questions of the challenge: what is changing, where, how much (change per decade with a 95% confidence interval) and whether the change is significant (two tests, corrected for autocorrelation and for multiple testing). This matters because a line that goes up is not always a real change: of 130 series, 101 look significant with a plain test and 74 remain after the corrections. The site keeps non-significant results on screen, flags records with known data problems, offers three reading levels (Everyone, Student, Researcher) and leaves the conclusion to the reader. It is a static site with no login and no server.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Keeling is a web globe (three.js, NASA Blue Marble surface) with twelve layers, one per NASA variable: precipitation, near-surface and 2 m air temperature, surface air temperature, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, total water vapor, tropospheric NO2, total ozone, UV aerosol index, vegetation greenness (NDVI) and land surface temperature. A visitor picks a place (five in Taiwan, twelve world cities, or the global mean), switches layers on, and plays a timeline through every month of the record. Particles follow the value of the selected month. For each variable an investigation panel has four tabs, one per question of the challenge: what is changing, where, how much, and is it significant. Each tab starts with a one-sentence answer generated from the results, then a chart. A global trend map shows the per-cell trend of seven variables.

HOW IT WORKS

  1. Fetch: point series, area means and 345 global monthly grid cubes (about 90 GB) through NASA Giovanni, Harmony, AppEEARS, POWER and Earthdata Cloud OPeNDAP.
  2. Unify: daily (OMI) and 8- or 16-day (MODIS) products are averaged to months, with the coverage of each month recorded. Every series is stored in one common format. Missing months stay missing; raw values are never overwritten.
  3. Statistics, the same for every series: monthly anomalies (each value minus the mean of its calendar month); least-squares trend per decade; 95% confidence interval and t-test with an effective sample size from the lag-1 autocorrelation; Mann-Kendall tests and the Theil-Sen slope; Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across all series.
  4. Publish: the results are static JSON files. The site reads them and does no test in the browser, so it needs no server and no login.

WHAT WE FOUND

Of 130 analysed series, 101 look significant with a plain test; 83 remain after the autocorrelation correction and 74 after the multiple-testing correction. GLDAS air temperature has step changes in May 2011, July 2017 and June 2019 (about +0.4, +0.6 and -0.6 K against MERRA-2), the months its input analysis was upgraded; its trend is shown with a caution mark and is not presented as a climate signal. Exploratory data mining (association rules, a variable network, similar series, decision trees) is reported with baselines: precipitation with soil moisture, and soil moisture with evapotranspiration, are correlated in all twelve world cities with the same sign; the decision trees did not beat simple baselines in walk-forward validation, and the site says so. Correlations are not presented as causes.

WHO IT IS FOR AND WHY IT IS DIFFERENT

It is for students and curious members of the public. Three reading levels (Everyone, Student, Researcher) change the wording and the amount of detail, never the numbers. Non-significant results stay on screen, because not significant is not the same as no change. Data companions, original characters drawn by code, walk a first-time visitor through the four questions. The interface can be used with the keyboard and respects the reduce-motion setting.

TOOLS

Data layer: Python 3.11+, uv, httpx, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, mlxtend, scikit-learn, netCDF4, rasterio; PostgreSQL 17 with TimescaleDB and PostGIS as a working database; SQLite export. Web: TypeScript, React 19, three.js, react-three-fiber, Vite. Tests: pytest and Vitest. Hosting: GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.

LIMITS

Outside Taiwan the site shows twelve cities and the global mean for ten of the twelve variables. A city value is one grid cell of the product, not a city boundary. The direction particles move in is illustrative (there is no wind data). Trends are linear only. The Japanese, German and French interface texts were translated by AI tools and not proofread by native speakers.

LINKS

Stable version pinned for this submission: https://nasa-hackathon-2026.github.io/earth-system-trend-detective/stable/

Latest version: https://nasa-hackathon-2026.github.io/earth-system-trend-detective/

Code, data documentation, methods and AI disclosure: https://github.com/nasa-hackathon-2026/earth-system-trend-detective

Pinned release with the cleaned database: https://github.com/nasa-hackathon-2026/earth-system-trend-detective/releases/tag/submission-2026-11-15

USE OF AI

The code, the tests and the documentation were written with AI coding tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) under the team's direction; the direction and the decisions are the team's. The layout and the factual text of the demo slides were also produced with an AI tool. No AI-generated image, video or audio is used; the characters are drawn by program code and the globe images are NASA imagery. Details are in the README of the repository.

OMI OMTO3d v003 - total column ozone
OMI OMAERUVd v003 - UV aerosol index
MODIS Terra MOD13A3 v061 - vegetation greenness (NDVI), monthly
MODIS Terra MOD13Q1 v061 - vegetation greenness (NDVI), 16-day 250 m
MODIS Terra MOD11A2 v061 - daytime land surface temperature
NASA Giovanni (time-series API and averaging service)
NASA Earthdata (CMR, Harmony, Earthdata Cloud OPeNDAP)
NASA POWER monthly API (cross-check of MERRA-2 temperature)
NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP) v4
SMAP L3 SPL3SMP V009 (evaluated for Taiwan, not used)
NASA Visible Earth - The Blue Marble (globe surface image)
NASA GIBS - Blue Marble shaded relief (close views)
Acker et al. 2009, SeaWiFS chlorophyll time series (NASA NTRS, challenge resource)

NOAA NCEI GHCN-Monthly v4 (Menne et al. 2018)

NIST CCCBDB (bond lengths and angles in the close-up views)
